To address the rising number of bicycle-related accidents, this paper introduces a novel approach for real-time detection of bicycle riders in traffic, with the ultimate goal of enhancing their safety. A computer vision system is designed to identify responsible parties in traffic accidents, with a specific focus on bicycle riders. The proposed system combines a deep learning model with a customized data set, implemented on an embedded device with sufficient processing power. The integration of a context-sensitive framework enables seamless tracking of bicycle riders across various scenes, with the use of a distinct identifier for accurate video-based tracking. With the capabilities of achieving approximately 56 frames per second on a JAEUS-ODI board, this system is well-suited for accurate hazard prediction in real-time, with the ability to distinguish between a variety of bicycle-related threats. A comprehensive evaluation of the proposed model reveals a remarkable mAP50 of 44.4%, with 70.9% mAP50 for horizontal-oriented bicycles, with further plans for the development of a video analytics module to inform traffic participants of impending threats.

This research involves developing a novel robotic motion planning framework that integrates control barrier functions to ensure safe and adaptive navigation. The model consists of a conventional dynamic system, a control barrier function, and a feedback stabilization component. The control barrier function has been redefined with certain characteristics to simplify convergence and safety analysis, and its integration with a feedback stabilization component has been proven to result in robust stability and meet robustness conditions. The framework's capability has been demonstrated through simulation tests, including scenarios involving unpredictable environments, parameter variations, and distinct control structures. The results show that the motion planning framework generated adaptive and secure trajectories in response to dynamic changes and uncertainties.

For a finite ring R with p n elements where p is a prime number, the set S consists of all enrolling numbers of the form BP(R, p^r, n) where r varies over natural numbers. The product of the numbers in S divided by the highest common divisor of their elements results in an interesting limit L(R, p). The following conjecture is presented: if the ring R has p n entries and the prime p does not divide the coefficient part C of the Euler's totient function n, then the product of all enrolling numbers divided by the highest common divisor of their elements is equal to n. Based on the given hypothesis, many relationships, particularly Beatty's theorem, Frobenius' totient sum formula, and Cathcart's result, have been verified. Moreover, the presented method can also be employed to determine the product of all enrolling numbers divided by the highest common divisor of their elements for function fields. The proof of the conjecture for prime-square counting numbers relies on the work of Gelfond, Brauer localizations, and the concept called "self-duality".

Deep Neural Network (DNN) models are notoriously vulnerable to 'adversarial examples', which are input data carefully constructed to mislead DNN predictions and discover vulnerabilities in the model. While extensive research has to date focused on mitigating these failures from within the model itself, our study explores an innovative approach that incorporates knowledge from external sources. By leveraging multi-source and multi-modal knowledge databases such as KnowledgeGraph, we can enhance DNN resilience against adversarial examples without compromising their core structure. We develop novel techniques for integrating graph knowledge into DNN loss functions and verifying system robustness, which we then test using AdversarialRobustness-Vis's visualisation tools to compare performance before and after integration with knowledge from Wikidata. The results demonstrate a substantial improvement in DNN robustness against specific adversarial examples, which we then successfully generalize to multiple attack techniques and multiple knowledge databases. Moreover, through a stochastic process, we discover new 'adversarial examples' previously unknown to the model, which we then proceed to analyze. Our findings raise essential questions regarding natural resilience, current research focuses and the emerging paradigm of 'Knowledge Inside, Outside, Beyond' in the context of deep learning.

The nonlocal conservation laws with flux functions described through widely accepted nonanalytic and asymptotically analyzed functions have previously been shown to have self-similar solutions that reduce to the classical car-following model under specific conditions. This reduction relies on the nonanalytic nature of the function near zero being applicable in both directions, and we analyze the entropy admissibility of these self-similar solutions under these assumptions. We also investigate the rate of convergence of the solutions to the classical model and verify that the model is asymptotically stable under the specified conditions.

We introduce a general framework for describing the structural features of dilation surfaces and their associated saddle structures. A novel type of link, called a horizon saddle link, is defined, and it is proven that all dilation surfaces possess a universal, isotopically invariant collection of such links. It is further demonstrated that the configuration of these links determines key aspects of a dilation surface's topological characteristics, as well as the specific outcomes of its Saddle-Monotone transformation. In addition, an explicit algorithm is provided for determining the exact form of these transformations, along with the corresponding results of its classification.

Recent studies of brain networks have utilized total correlation to analyze functional brain connectivity, leading to the development of a comprehensive total correlation fingerprint for human cognition, which has been linked to various cognitive factors and brain structure. Building on this framework, we investigate the relationship between total correlation and the complexity of brain connectivity, and demonstrate that total correlation can effectively reveal the functional brain network, particularly in individuals with altered brain structure. Moreover, we validate the use of total correlation in resting-state fMRI analysis, thereby contributing to our understanding of the human brain's functional network and its association with individual differences.

The classical Segal-Bargmann transformation, a key object connecting phase space and Hilbert space, involves the Segal-Bargmann space, which represents the space of all square-integrable holomorphic functions on a phase space formed by identifying symmetric polynomials with elements of a Clifford algebra over R. This environment leads to a Clifford algebra-forming quantization, which corresponds to a part of a larger isomorphism, known as the Taylor isomorphism, that connects two Hilbert spaces. The SB transformation then transitions into a Clifford algebra-valued form by implementing a Clifford Fourier transform on SB space, which results in a space of square-integrable functions over a space of quadratic polynomials on a phase space formed by identifying self-adjoint elements of the Clifford algebra over R. This work examines the mathematical structure of the Clifford algebra-valued SB transformation.

In the context of Gaussian field theory, the concept of a field being conditioned upon another field is studied from a pathwise perspective. Unconditional weak convergence of the conditioning procedure is established for generalized field combinations that do not necessarily involve increasing fields. Specifically, the conditioning procedure involves dividing by a field's'standardization factor', which captures both a field's scaling and correlation properties. The theoretical findings are exemplified through a localization procedure based on the standardization factor, offering an alternative approach to conventional conditioning methods.

Ground-based sensing systems that utilize dense sensor nodes have shown great promise in environmental monitoring, but are limited by their need to be connected via wired or ground-based devices. This requires significant upfront costs and infrastructure for the sensors to function effectively. This paper introduces an innovative approach by establishing a wireless aerial linkage between ground-based sensors and existing aerial sensors, enabled through balloon or drone platforms that also serve as veritable satellite systems. The proposed architecture involves balancing data transmission, system resource allocation, and routing problems, and we begin to explore its feasibility through simulations using real-world data and scenarios from both the drone and balloon perspectives.

The discovery of neutrino oscillations led to the understanding that flavor change is a fundamental aspect of particle physics. The phenomenon not only presents an interesting application of special relativity, but also sheds light on how particles acquire mass. Over the past two decades, research into neutrino oscillations has refined our understanding of neutrino physics. Theoretical models indicate the likelihood of a new, high-energy regime of neutrino physics being discovered at the next generation of experiments. Current studies focus on fundamental neutrino properties, such as mass hierarchy and mixing angles. A major project, the Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE), is underway to explore these aspects at precision levels. DUNE consists of four neutrino detectors placed at different distances from powerful neutron decay sources at the Fermilab National Accelerator Laboratory. The project, with its predicted high-fidelity capabilities and ability to record and analyze vast amounts of data, is expected to make significant contributions to mass hierarchy measurements and precision measurements of neutrino oscillation. This presentation will explore DUNE's capabilities and methods for advancing neutrino physics research.

In high-energy physics, identifying top quarks within complex event data is a crucial task. Tagging algorithms for top quarks utilize machine learning models, which have limitations when dealing with high-pT topologies. A novel top tagging algorithm, referred to as enhanced top tagging (ETT), has been developed by combining a set of simple top tagging rules. Through its convolutional neural network (CNN) transformation, it is demonstrated that ETT can be represented as a portion of a larger, more complex neural network model. Utilizing the Shapley value method, which aims to determine the individual contributions of these basic components, it was found that ETT mainly consists of sub-networks performing sub-top tagging operations. Furthermore, with some modifications, it was shown that ETT can be integrated into a larger neural network model, potentially enhancing its overall performance.
This document introduces the process of formally representing and advanced veto groups within organizations, followed by verification and refinement concepts within those representations.

A crucial factor in achieving consistent reinforcement learning results involves
significant interaction with a diverse and representative environment, which
can be efficiently accomplished using experience replay. Although previously
deemed insignificant in reinforcement learning, the importance of replaying
varied scenarios has recently been recognized. The key factor influencing the
efficiency of experience replay lies in its ability to reduce variability across
different replays. Current techniques, such as the uniform method, directly
assign weights to each scenario without considering its relevance to current
optimization processes. In contrast, statistical methods like standard deviation
focus on scenario variability but fail to account for dynamic scenario distributions
during progressive learning. This study introduces a novel variance diminution
approach, $VD^2$, which dynamically adjusts the replay weights of scenarios
based on their relative impact on policy optimization. By incorporating the
 covariance matrix of temporal differences, $VD^2$ effectively diminishes the
variability of experience replay, leading to accelerated learning and robustness
against noisy data. Our experiments on multiple continuous control tasks
demonstrate the efficacy of $VD^2$ in boosting policy optimization with both
noisy and existing experience repositories.

Two new methods, the superbosonization technique and the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation, have been proposed to deal with the difficulties encountered in Gaussian integrations where the matrices are odd or mixed in nature. This research investigates the similarities between these two methods by applying, for example, to the free fermion theory where the result can be verified analytically. It's found that the application of these methods is not equivalent, rather, they are complementary and can be used depending on the specific situation the system encounters. Notably, the superbosonization technique is generally more straightforward and efficient. Furthermore, this study also found that the effective action derived from the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation for the free fermion system is inconsistent, resulting in incorrect matrix elements, whereas the superbosonization technique yields a correct result. On the other hand, the superbosonization technique is found to be inconsistent when applied to the free Majorana fermion system, using an example provided in the study. It's found that the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation is more suitable for systems with odd Gaussian integrations.

This paper addresses a crucial question in the field of building occupant comfort prediction: how does motion in a space affect its thermal comfort? To answer this, we first collect detailed sensor data from an experimental building over five months. Then, we use our concept of motion aspects to analyze how people move around within a space and its impact on thermal comfort. These motion aspects reveal a correlation between how people spatially interact and the thermal comfort of a space. Next, we create a novel mathematical transformation to represent the dynamic relationship between different areas of a space. These results can inform building designers and managers to improve the comfort of a space by understanding how motion affects its thermal comfort. This paper showcases a new way of looking at how motion influences different aspects of a space and its implications for building design and management. It also introduces a relevant statistical model for researchers to explore other types of motion and its relationships.

This research focuses on efficiently integrating managed C data into embedded C programs by employing both Rust and JavaScript. An embedded C program allocates C data for subsequent use by a managed component, written in Rust, which is then accessed through a compatible interface. The paper introduces a verification-based approach to ensure embedded C programs correctly manage their embedded Rust data. Additionally, it outlines a practical library providing JavaScript access to these shared Rust data structures while ensuring the safety of sensitive data. Finally, the paper confirms the validity of our approach by detailing the development process of a prototype system using JavaScript and Rust, and demonstrating this technology on a specific use case involving a microcontroller.

We explore neutrinoless double-beta decay mediated by a pair of Majorana particles other than neutrinos, such as those within the Higgs sector or elsewhere, in the context of the Large Hadron Collider. To do this, we venture into uncharted territory by creating a novel process where two heavy particles are produced together in a single step, rather than each one being created separately. Our investigation focuses particularly on the production of these pairs at the Large Hadron Collider through both the Standard Model and beyond, with two specific scenarios being considered - one involving the production of two heavy scalars resulting from a Majorana Yukawa coupling, and another where two components of a mixed state are produced where one part is primarily Standard Model-like while also including a small amount of a Majorana component. In both scenarios, we look at how these produced heavy states can decay into a pair of Standard Model gauge bosons, such as W bosons or Z bosons, with such processes being influenced by a variety of factors including whether the states involved are purely Standard Model-based or also influenced by the presence of Majorana components. In addition to these considerations, we also reflect on the importance of analyzing not only final state momenta but also the spins and other properties of the particles involved, with the use of colliders offering a means to study these parameters directly.

Recent advancements in polar code decoding have seen the introduction of belief propagation list decoding, offering a compromise between error rate and delay. However, the performance of belief propagation list decoding depends heavily on the size of the list, making it challenging to determine an optimal list size. In this research, a novel approach based on a polar subcode is presented to specify the size of the list. By dividing the polar code into multiple subcodes, each with a shorter length, is shown to be equivalent to a subcode-coded polar code. These subcodes can be decoded in an iterative manner using successive cancellation density evolution and linear decoding. The performance of the subcode method is evaluated through simulations and the results demonstrate that the size of the list can be determined efficiently and effectively. Additionally, the size of the list is found to be closely related to the subcode performance, offering a possible design method for belief propagation list decoding.

Images obtained from telescopes can be described by a specific point spread function (PSF) that defines how well the instrument can form precise images. By re-examining the concept of deconvolution in astronomy, we suggest a novel approach to determine the PSFs of multiple telescopes, even when their images are merged. This methodology does not rely on a single calibration image with an known PSF. Instead, it relies solely on observations of combined images source positions. Our comprehensive analysis demonstrates that these observations can be used to establish a set of matrices that effectively invert the action of any linear system. As a result, we derive a general algorithm that allows us to determine the PSFs of individual telescopes, even when their positions and orientations relative to each other are known. Furthermore, our approach also considers the potential distortions present in the combined images. To validate the effectiveness and practicality of this method, we conducted thorough simulations and applied it to actual astronomical images of the bright planet Jupiter taken with a combination of telescopes in Paris and Sydney.

The fracture strength of solid crystals is examined and calculated using their elastic constants. Typically, the critical strength of a solid material ranges between a few hundred to a few thousand Megapascals. There is no notable correlation between a solid's fracture strength and its elastic modulus, however these two values do share a connection when considering the shear modulus. Most solid crystals have a fracture strength close to their shear moduli. This study demonstrates that if a solid's fracture exhibits elastic behavior then its fracture strength is predicted to be around 50% of its shear modulus squared, in line with earlier studies. If, however, a solid's fracture does not exhibit elastic behavior then a variety of values can be predicted based on the elastic constants. Furthermore, this study identifies characteristics of solid crystals that are naturally resistant to fractures.

We establish the connection between the driven Gaussian free surface and the multiplicative family of Conformal Field Theories based on Schramm-Holland's multiple SLE. This relationship enables us to directly map the O(N)-symmetric Gaussian free field to the multiple SLE_{k,N} based on the O(N)-invariant Brownian motion. Furthermore, the O(N)-symmetric Gaussian free field is related to the multiple SLE_{k,N} that is driven by the O(N)-invariant Dyson model. Lastly, the latter is shown to be equivalent to the multiple SLE_{k,N} driven by the DOXX process, providing an alternative proof to the direct connection between the DOXX and XXZ spin chain recently established by Lee and Yang.

In this research, we address the Cauchy problem for the Navier-Stokes equations in multi-dimensional space with smooth periodic initial conditions and obtain analytical estimates of the solution's maximum norm and its derivative's maximum norm over time and spatial coordinates.

The increasing use of quantum computers in near-term computing has led to a growing need for testing and verification procedures that can handle noisy quantum gates and faulty measurements efficiently. In our research, we have developed an innovative approach based on the Peckey inequality to verify classical descriptions of quantum processes. Our method allows for the evaluation of correctly prepared quantum states and classical decisions following certain measurements within a linear time complexity, namely O(n^2). This breakthrough is made possible by leveraging Grover's algorithm, which facilitates more efficient search and verification procedures. Additionally, we have adapted our technique to handle general quantum operations that involve two qubit interactions, but with increased runtime complexity at O(n^3). Although this is still a significant improvement over previous verification methods, which ran at O(n^4), it is unclear at present whether our linear time complexity can be further optimized for specific problem cases.

A chain of blockchain technology guarantees the unaltered sequence of transaction records, offering transparency and tamper-evidence. In the context of Internet of Things (IoT), blockchain offers a secure recording system. However, applying blockchain directly to IoT devices is impractical. This study proposes an innovative blockchain framework integrated with a smart contract management system, using an oracle network to refresh static data on blockchain platforms. The proposed framework is demonstrated through a food supply chain example.

Generative models for cellular shapes can be utilized in multiple applications, 
such as completing partial cell images and creating synthetic cell models for 
simulations. Due to the intricate topological features of cells, it is crucial 
that a model can capture these complex structures effectively. Traditional 
methods, like mesh-based and point-set representations, have limitations in 
handling these complex cases. In this research, we propose a mesh-free, 
implicit geometry model based on signed distance functions, which can model 
cells of various morphologies. Our approach involves supervising the signed 
distance function representation using two loss functions: a reconstruction 
loss that measures the accurate rendering of cell contours and an embedding 
loss that ensures correct structural understanding of cell shapes through 
segmentation of regions behind the signed distance function. Our model can 
generate cells with complex topological features, but it also has the ability 
to construct cells with simple morphologies by constraining the signed 
distance function values for specific regions. Furthermore, we present a 
novel loss function that utilizes diffusion maps to identify and analyze the 
cell's structural components from both its surface and interior. These 
diffusion maps can be employed to create a coherent understanding of a cell's 
morphology by mapping intricate features to a set of interpretable, high-level 
descriptions. Our model with the combined loss functions outperforms other 
point-set and mesh-based methods in both synthesis and editing tasks.

Individuals who are print-handicapped or print-temporarily are severely
disadvantaged when interacting with digital documents, having to rely on
assistance from sighted guides. Our investigation emphasizes the great need
for digitally rendering document accessibility independently of printing
purposes. Specifically, we highlight how being print impaired hinders one's
ability to effectively mark up and organize documents, thus necessitating
a special consideration in document design. Building on this insight, we
propose an innovative interactive system, called Inks in Focus, aimed at
redressing print impairment during collaborative work on digital documents.

While BERT excels in many NLP tasks, it has a significant limitation: it only considers one direction of token relationships in each token's representation. We have developed XLNet, an enhanced pretraining approach that surpasses BERT's capabilities by incorporating autoregressive modeling in both forward and reverse directions through interleaved token ordering. We achieve this through the use of an autoregressive language model, using an orthogonal sampling strategy to overcome the issues associated with parallel sampling in bidirectional pretraining. We have conducted thorough evaluations of our method on 20 tasks across 20 datasets, and the results demonstrate XLNet's superiority; notably, in approximately 50% of the task-assessment pairs XLNet's performance significantly outperformed the state-of-the-art. We have based our comparisons with the most advanced BERT variants, such as Google's multi-task BERT and BERT variants with masked LM pretraining. We have also released XLNet's implementation at https://github.com/thomasbray/X-Let.

We've developed an approach to analyse transit spectroscopy data, and we've found that stellar activity significantly affects our ability to detect atmospheric signals in low-resolution spectra. To counter this, we've identified suppression techniques that can separate the effects of stellar activity and star-orbital factors. Our research involves real-world data from GJ 1214 b and BD-10 j b using the Second Epoch Telescope on Mauna Kea, and we've tested various strategies including high-resolution spectroscopy with the HIRES instrument. Our analysis shows that with HRSS data, stellar activity signals in the star GJ 1214 are clearly defined, unlike in the low-resolution LRSS data where the signals become blended with star-orbital effects. Using simulated data from various planets with low- and high-temperature atmospheres, we've tested the effectiveness of high-resolution spectroscopy in detecting atmospheric signals behind GJ 1214. Our analysis reveals that with HRSS data, we can consistently identify atmospheric signals at a 3-sigma confidence level as late as 5-6 planetary radii, and in the case of GJ 1214 b using both HRSS and LRSS we failed to detect any atmospheric signals at a 3-sigma confidence level. Our analysis also reveals that with HRSS data, we can partially detect atmospheric signals at a 2-sigma confidence level in the case of H2O and CO through absorption, and in the case of a temperature signal at a 2

This paper develops a flexible approach to a discrete version of the uniform curvature metrics initially proposed by Taubes. The approach is adapted to fit a general class of extended Riemann surfaces featuring singularities, incorporating extended surfaces with boundaries and singularities that have a one-dimensional fibration. Extended surfaces can feature any number of singularities that fit specific criteria, and these criteria include non-forking points and a specified type of boundary behavior. A particular example of extended surfaces featuring a significant type of singularity is the fibration of a Riemann surface over a specific polygon. A notable subcategory of these surfaces includes conformally positively curved Riemann surfaces featuring a significant type of singularity called edge singularities. These edge singularities have a specific tangent behavior and conform to a specific curvature bound, and they also feature a unique metric that behaves in a specific way within a particular region. A notable example of conformally positively curved Riemann surfaces is the del Pezzo surfaces featuring a specific type of singularity called odd smoothness singularities, and these surfaces feature a specific curvature bound within a specific region. A particular example of a conformally positively curved Riemann surface featuring a specific type of boundary behavior is the blowups of a projective plane that features a specific type of boundary behavior called an N-fold surface. A note is also provided to distinguish this new approach from a previous version of the uniform curvature metric introduced by the author, and this previous version is more restrictive than the new

Research into the swimming motion of the centipede forficatus near the surface of water-water interface shows it doesn't use its 14 leg pairs primarily for movement; instead of most aquatic animals that move by creating waves along the body, this species moves using waves in the opposite direction, from tail to head. Its low mass and the presence of fluids against its body cause movement dynamics where drag forces overcome inertia, which can be explained using theories initially based on microorganisms. These theories are applicable to larger animals, which challenges the existing idea that size significantly impacts locomotion methods.

A novel from 2018 titled "The Last Tsunami Ocean" prompted the author, leading to an exploration of the most significant factors influencing the dispersal distance of a tsunami raised by an asteroid impact. This involves solving the linear dispersion equation with a steady-state approach, along with identifying key factors that impact the tsunami wave's maximum amplitude at a certain distance. Furthermore, an approximation was developed for predicting the peak amplitude of a highly dispersive wave at any desired location. This analysis led to an understanding of how various factors affect the tsunami wave's behavior at different points. The findings were then used to devise an approach for selecting time and spatial step sizes that ensure accuracy in simulating an asteroid-generated tsunami. The author also presents the results of dispersal equation precision tests using both arbitrary and uniform distributions of source spectrum.

Recent observations from the JWST have uncovered a subset of galaxies that are extremely luminous in the infrared, yet undetectable in optical observations. These galaxies are critical players in the process of reheating, which occurs during the epoch of reionization and is highly influential on the dynamics of hydrogen. By analyzing data collected by the JWST, a new sample of 27 galaxies has been generated, which are found to be predominantly classified as star-forming galaxies with stellar masses ranging from approximately 8e6 to 11e6 times that of the sun. By presenting the initial analysis and findings of these galaxies, further research into the characteristics of high-redshift galaxies can be conducted, which may lead to a greater understanding of the mechanisms driving hydrogen reionization and reheating.

We expand upon the seven-dimensional gravity framework initially explored by Smolyanov and Sachdev, adding a pure geometrical term to the theory. The earlier model was characterized by a seven-dimensional Riemann curvature tensor. In the present study, an additional pure geometrical term is incorporated, composed of the square of the seven-dimensional self-dual tensor field strength and the square of the seven-dimensional Hodge dual of the self-dual tensor. The additional term's inclusion is facilitated by the use of a modified topological trick. The resulting theory, resulting from the most preferred choice of parameters, exhibits U(1) gauge invariance and possesses a Lagrangian resembling the six-dimensional (2,0) theory. The resulting theory also displays AdS_7 x S^0 spacetime vacua and mirror symmetry between the matter and gravity sectors. The maximum allowed parameter value yields a conformal invariance of the massless W_3 spinor field, a spin-1/2 field, and three spin-3/2 fields, similar to those seen in six-dimensional (1,0) and (2,0) theories. The resulting theory is also used to study supersymmetric quantum field theories.

We are given a specific type of blocked disk arrangement in a channel with alternating lengths and weights, and we need to determine the extremal configurations consisting of two different disk sizes. This problem extends previous research by Serra and Zeros on alternating sequences of blocked disks in a channel, and it builds upon previous studies regarding blocked disks in a channel by Arseny Arshakov, Vladimir Arshakov, and Mikhail Krutikov. To solve this issue, we utilize a modified version of the maximum principle for strips established by Arshakov. Our research also leads to two related questions involving larger rectangles with alternating corners. These questions may be difficult to solve using the maximum principle, particularly when it comes to establishing exact values, so we formulate them as integer programming problems. However, we currently lack a solution to this problem. To better understand the relationship between large and small blocked disks in a strip, we consider a scenario where very large disks are present and try to prove that small disks can reach a maximum height if and only if a specific region, which we call the Arshakov corridor, is completely filled with small disks. This assumption is based on previous research by Arshakov as well as on the effective use of the maximum principle for strips. Two extreme flavors of the El Ni\~no Southern Oscillation (ENSO), characterized by alternating patterns of warm and cold temperatures in the central Pacific, have been identified as significant indicators of global precipitation patterns. A study analyzed global downscaling models to predict seasonal precipitation around the world from ENSO indices, and found two prominent flavors of ENSO (PMI and LI) in addition to the well-known El Ni\~no (EP) and La Ni\~na (LN) patterns. These four flavors (EP, LI, PMI, and LN) were linked to varying patterns of precipitation around the world, with the largest fluctuations observed in South America, Africa, and the southern hemisphere. Interestingly, the LI flavor of ENSO, characterized by excessive rainfall in the AGCM by its negative index, was found to leave a distinctive mark on global precipitation patterns. A deeper analysis of these ENSO flavors and their impacts on precipitation in key regions, particularly in India and Australia, revealed significant and ongoing trends related to these ENSO flavors, highlighting their importance in predicting seasonal precipitation around the world.

In various fields of science and technology, soft materials are used to create different forms of structural protrusions on their surface. For example, these phenomena are observed at the surface of gel layers exposed to external forces, the introduction of foreign substances into a gel, and the growth of crystalline lattices on an amorphous substrate. Our experiment involves measuring the scattering of gel-forming mixtures exposed to uniaxial compaction, and then analyzing the obtained results to describe the early stages of elongated particle arrangement using a theoretical model for aligned multilayered films. By applying this approach, we were able to determine that the thickness at which the arrangement becomes affine depends on two factors: the polymerization degree of fibrins formed during the compaction and the viscosity of these fibrins. Our findings also show that by combining light scattering with factors such as light intensity, wavelength, and angle, it is possible to obtain detailed information about the internal structure of these materials at different length scales. As a result, our study proposes a new technique using laser spectroscopy to detect and analyze the early stages of elongated particle arrangement in real-time.

This research focuses on a population model to analyze the impact of environmental toxicity on a single species that adapts and ages, also taking into consideration behavioral interactions. A comprehensive mathematical framework is developed to examine the long-term outcomes of this population under various environmental conditions, focusing on the effects of pollution. A key aspect of this model involves a population sub-group that interacts with its surroundings in a way that influences the environment's toxicity level, creating a feedback effect that affects population dynamics. To understand how adaptation and aging affect population growth, a set of ordinary linear differential equations is employed to model the population's density over time, with equation coefficients representing population growth rate, behavior influenced by the environment's toxicity, adaptation, and aging factors. A population growth rate criterion is established to determine the long-term outcomes of this model, and numerical representations are used to illustrate and validate the model's equations.

The research expands upon the decision procedures recently discovered for certain subvariant logics, specifically focusing on the decidable and complexity aspects of Weakening and Contraction Hypersequent Subsequentical Logics. Their new decision methods involve leveraging the previously established results from their parent logics, while also yielding further complexity information. The research further contributes by demonstrating that certain of these logics have computationally intractable complexity, specifically being NP-hard, using a constructed reduction from a known NP-hard problem. The research provides an additional insight by revealing that all (unbounded) weakening logics with finite binary fusion are actually weakening logics with finite binary fusion without the right weakening property. The research's main contribution is an analysis of the decidability and complexity of so-called 'BCHSPLs', a class which encompasses all the considered Weakening and Contraction Hypersequent Subsequentical Logics. The research's study of BCHSPLs allows it to generalize various previously established results about the class. The research further uses the established results from BCHSPLs to tackle a long-standing question about the (unfair) game-theoretical interpretation of Public Announcements. The research's study of BCHSPLs is grounded in an analysis of the (unbounded) weakening logics with finite binary fusion, a specific subclass of BCHSPLs. This research presents HyperExpan, the first hyperbolic neural network for hierarchical concept expansion, a task that involves relating concepts to their broader categories to replicate human concept extension abilities. Hierarchical concepts in this context facilitate a more efficient integration of training data and address issues related to hyperbolic neural network scaling. Hyperbexpans' architecture captures complex concept relationships, offering a more accurate representation in higher-dimensional hyperbolic space. Evaluation on publicly available datasets demonstrates that HyperExpan surpasses the performance of prior research and hyperbolic hierarchical concept expansion methods, also surpassing results from non-hyperbolic neural networks. Additionally, this study analyzes the effects of varying hyperbolic learning algorithms and embedding dimensions on concept expansion performance, providing insights into the interactions between these variables.

The interaction between two molecules is influenced by an external electric field. This phenomenon, known as the polarizable continuum model, temporarily allocates charge to the molecules, causing a significant environmental impact. The effect of the environmental charge on intermolecular interactions is a topic of research, and this study aims to explore this issue by focusing on the behavior of non-covalent interactions in electric fields. The assessment involves comparing theoretical models, including a monopole model, against a more sophisticated approach that accounts for the distribution of dipoles and quadrupoles. The results reveal that there is a viable strategy for developing a new theoretical model that accurately describes non-covalent interactions in electric fields, thereby enabling the creation of a more refined model with improved accuracy. The proposed model can be used in future studies, and it has been effectively demonstrated using the S66 dataset, which includes a wide range of non-covalent interactions. The assessment against the established Aubert-Carlier-Salez (ACS) basis set highlights the significance of including the ACS term in the model, and this conclusion is supported by an analysis of intermolecular energy patterns in the studied dataset.

The fourth Industrial Revolution has significantly transformed manufacturing systems, introducing conceptual and physical data management platforms that facilitate real-time decision-making through advanced analytics. Despite their limitations, current approaches struggle to account for certain types of uncertainty. This issue is likely a result of the widespread belief among researchers and practitioners that uncertainty only applies to specific instances. This misconception may impede the development of innovative solutions in Industrial Automation. This work seeks to clarify the distinct definitions of randomness and uncertainty, highlighting their interrelation in the context of probabilistic networks. We then examine the benefits and drawbacks of models that fail to accommodate non-deterministic uncertainty and propose a novel framework that integrates Markov Field Trees with both deterministic and stochastic dependencies. This approach aims to improve scheduling outcomes in the Industry 4.0 sector by addressing non-deterministic uncertainty.

A key requirement in Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS) is that they remain functional despite potential disruptions, referred to as cyber-physical disruptions. This concept has been the focus of research, but current understandings of resilience in CPS are limited due to subjectivity and a lack of standardized definitions. This study proposes a resilience framework grounded in a specific logic used for specifying requirements in CPS, a particular language called STL. This framework offers a practical approach to measuring CPS resilience in the face of cyber-photical disruptions and has the added benefit of allowing for easy modification and adjustments to the system's resilience level. Additionally, this framework can serve as a useful tool for testing and evaluating CPS properties and is compatible with existing models.

A hotly debated topic in modern particle physics is the possibility of dark matter composed of feebly interacting small black holes, which could be detected by the gravitational waves they produce.  Since these gravitational waves have extremely long ranges and masses that can vary greatly, a local search for this dark matter, which is part of the dark matter consisting of light and small black holes, is possible.  The possibility of discovering this dark matter using a network of advanced sensors, particularly those that can measure acceleration, is an area of research worth exploring.  Theoretical predictions based on this scenario, which is referred to as a ground-based gravitational search for dark matter consisting of light and small black holes, have been developed and are currently being studied.  As part of this research, a specific scenario was studied in which a large network of advanced high-sensitivity accelerometers place constraints on the abundance of such small black holes.  The results from this research, which includes the specific results when using Hanford, Livingston, and Pyhasalmi as part of the network, is an important step in the search for this dark matter and serves as a representative example of what can be accomplished with a larger, global network of advanced high-sensitivity accelerometers.

We're focusing on the interior of a complete, non-compact Riemannian manifold with a specific structure, like the flat Euclidean space in higher dimensions, and we're studying a specific type of differential equation involving the diffusion of a signal over this manifold. This type of equation, known as the MBO aggregation equation, has been utilized extensively in various applications and its solution helps us understand the signal's spreading behavior. Due to technical difficulties associated with approximating the differential equation, as well as the challenges involved in analyzing its wide-ranging applications, we're able to derive precise estimates of the differences between approximate and exact solutions. These estimates help us derive precise time and spatial bounds for the approximation error, thereby providing significant insights into the behavior of the signal's diffusion. As a result, our findings enable us to generalize previously established theories for flat Euclidean space to more real-world scenarios of interest. Furthermore, our approximations help us derive precise, useful bounds on the behavior of the signal's diffusion in complex geometric settings, like those encountered in the study of diffusions on graphs from a manifold perspective.

By analyzing large X-ray flux scales, researchers have found that faint radio sources exhibit enhanced excess temperature and surface density compared to their radio counterparts. In addition, these faint radio sources display higher sub-mm to radio spectral indices. The discovery of their enhanced X-ray emission suggests that there are more low-jet power objects like the binary system SS433/HO 1345-646 that are not typically classified as compact jets. Alternatively, it is also possible that jet powers are dispersed throughout the population, resulting in jet powers that are relatively low yet still detectable. Our findings from the Parkes-ATCA Survey for CRRs suggest an association between these radio sources and galaxy nuclei, further indicating that they may be powered by low-jet powers. Our observations from the Parkes-ATCA Survey for CRRs also present an alternative explanation for the high excess temperature of these radio sources, stating it can be found in jets much longer than 1 parsec. In a previous study on the Parkes-ATCA Survey for CRRs it has been discovered that low-jet powers are linked to higher jet lengths. Therefore it is possible for the high excess temperature of these radio sources to be explained by identifying them as high-excess-temperature non-relativistic jets that are not typically classified as powerful CRTs.

Hidden Markov Models are a foundational tool in modeling intricate probabilistic systems. Yet, the models fail to accurately represent scenarios involving partial knowledge of a system's state, necessitating additional quantitative information which the classic HMMs cannot define. To address this limitation, Abstract Hidden Markov Models are introduced, providing a comprehensive framework that incorporates information theories to model Partially Observable Markov Processes. AHMMs can express both probabilistic and information-theoretic relationships between states, enabling a direct comparison between probabilistic and information-theoretic transitions. The models' equivalence to a monadic description makes them well-suited for denotational semantics in probabilistic programming. AHMMs can be extended to model Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes with a detailed structure, representing the observability of states. The proposed approach is practical, as shown through its application in analyzing a simple, real-world system. Furthermore, this method is recognized in the field of denotational semantics, with notable implications for the language language-hat.

We demonstrate that statistically nonlocality is a inherent characteristic of general, nonreversible continua that operate according to the second principles of thermodynamics, as opposed to reversible systems. Examples of continua that fall under this category include polymer and liquid crystals, which display a range of interesting behaviors due to their complex interactions with their environments. By examining the requirements for a continuum model to possess both thermodynamic consistency and statistical nonlocality, we aim to provide a clear understanding of this phenomenon and its implications for theoretically framing and empirically verifying models of nonreversible systems.

We introduce a novel framework for extending unitarity and applying the optimal scattering phenomenology to a broad range of theories beyond the Standard Model, utilizing an effective field theory approach with local operators up to a specified dimension. By implementing the generalized optical theorem related to scattering cross-sections, and incorporating a universal universal scattering function description, this framework enables a straightforward connection between couplings and scattering properties. We demonstrate the practical application of this phenomenological framework in analyzing scattering data, and show how it can be used to model scattering behavior in various theories without explicit field representations. Specifically, we are able to generate effective field theory equations for standard sectors like Higgs physics, compositeness, and dark matter, as well as more complex sector-based models such as two Higgs doublets, little Higgs, and warped extra-dimensions. This scattering-based phenomenology has the potential to reveal novel physics at future facilities with high energy and luminosity, such as those proposed for the FASER$\nu$ and CETA experiments.

This paper presents a comprehensive study of the characteristics of a blackbody in the presence of the Casimir effect, using both relativistic and non-relativistic approaches. We establish the electromagnetic field's temperature dependence, vector potential, and related thermodynamic quantities, including energy density, pressure, and heat transfer, under the influence of the Casimir effect. Notably, our thermodynamic relations and transport mechanisms align with standard blackbody behavior in the limit where Casimir contributions are negligible. We observe that the Casimir effect induces temperature-dependent modifications in energy density and pressure that are proportional to the temperature, while the heat transfer rate exhibits logarithmic temperature variations. Moreover, the Casimir effect has opposing signs in both the non-relativistic and relativistic contexts.

A possible approach to safeguarding location data privacy utilizes a secure random lattice transformation combined with a publicly available, statistically-related encoding method. While this method has been demonstrated to offer strong privacy protections as evidenced by its low location differential privacy guarantee, it has been observed to induce significant variability in the resulting location data for specific scenarios. To mitigate this issue, we introduce a novel privacy protocol, incorporating a publicly available probability distribution, referred to as the conditional prior, to refine the encoding result. The proposed research provides a comprehensive explanation of the proposed protocol, including its potential applications, its formal analysis using the information-theoretic concept of location differential privacy, and an experimental demonstration highlighting its effectiveness and high privacy guarantee.

A crucial task in autonomous robotics is localizing 3D point clouds, especially when using LiDAR data. The conventional method involves describing key frames and query points in a learned feature space and using a transformer network to compute their similarity. To improve this process, the Normal Distribution Transform (NDT) representation, which accurately captures 3D surface characteristics, is used for feature learning in this paper. The proposed NDT-Transformer integrates the NDT representation with a transformer network, demonstrating superior performance in large-scale point cloud localization experiments under real-world conditions, especially when dealing with partial overlaps between views. The proposed system outperformed state-of-the-art approaches using LiDAR-only data in a simulated indoor environment and achieved competitive results when combined with camera data in a mixed LiDAR-cameras scenario. Additionally, the proposed system demonstrated more efficient processing of data with complex structures.

Determining the optimal spatial resolution for resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) is a crucial yet unresolved issue. We undertook a comprehensive investigation to address this question by advancing a previous approach that leverages statistical power. We generated a database of 1000 analysis sets by simulating multiple resting-state network types and various mind sizes. We then used multiple criteria, including correlation decay rate, network localization, and spatial distribution characteristics, to evaluate the analysis sets. We selected the optimal spatial resolution for each network based on its spatial distribution. We evaluated the statistical significance of the resulting connections using non-parametric statistical methods and found the connections to be highly consistent with those observed in human brain data. We observed that higher spatial resolution generally resulted in more extensive connectivity, but with increasing resolution, the connectivity became less restricted to the relevant resting-state brain networks. We observed notable increases in connectivity related to the larger brain areas, including the cerebellum, the thalamus, and the white matter, as well as the parietal cortex. Our study provides new insights into the analysis of fMRI data, specifically the multi-scale analysis with respect to spatial resolution, which is highly relevant to understanding the human brain.

This paper maintains a sequential data structure allowing a network of processes to store and manage a sequence of names, accompanied by corresponding counter values. The proposed solution ensures that when a name is added to the data structure, its associated counter value remains unchanged. We have developed an energy-efficient algorithm utilizing a single process, which enables a sequential name addition operation without changing the counter value in about O(log^2 n) rounds, while conventional solutions require O(n^2) rounds. Furthermore, the developed algorithm is energy-efficient as it minimizes the use of beeps from the nodes involved, particularly, it reduces the beeps from new nodes by a factor of n compared to previous approaches. Another contribution is the development of an alternative algorithm that enables a sequential name addition operation in O(n * log^2 n) rounds or less, which is comparable to the performance of the latest energy-efficient algorithms for sequential name addition proposed in (Moses, Ritzenthaler, Schott, 2022).

Recent advances in NLP for code-mixed text have been notable, but using fixed approaches across diverse language scenarios has proven to be ineffective due to varying levels of intermingling of the constituent languages. For instance, code-mixed text in languages such as Punjabi-English exhibits significant language intermixture, whereas code-mixed text in languages such as Marathi-English has minimal intermixture. As a result, a fixed approach that excels in one scenario may fall short in another. To address these challenges, we suggest a novel Switching Point Based Adaptive (SPBA) model that adapts to the characteristics of individual language pairs throughout the training process. Our model, PESTO, relieves developers from manually configuring hyperparameters. Moreover, PESTO's cross-switching adaptation ensures that it can perform well on datasets from both highly mixed and minimally mixed language pairs. Our empirical analysis reveals that SPBA has the potential to enhance cross-lingual text representation for code-mixed language modeling, and our experiments using PESTO demonstrate superior performance on datasets from multiple language pairs at various mixing levels. Moreover, PESTO's source code is available for public use at https://github.com/asharake/PESTO.

Our calculations of the electronic structure, density of states, and critical temperature of H$_3$S as a function of pressure reveal a significant influence of a van Hove singularity (VHS) on the superconducting transition temperature $T_c$. Near the critical pressure of 155 GPa, where $T_{C}$ reaches its maximum at 287 K, the VHS maximizes the isotope effect and the density of states, ultimately controlling the pressure dependence of $T_C$ and its maximum value. The presence of the VHS also correlates with an enhanced pairing mechanism involving phonons in the H-S bond. The experimentally measured 150 GPa-$T_{Cmax}$ correlation in H$_3$S can also be seen in other hydrides like H$_3$Se, which however does not have the VHS effect. This however, suggests the possibility of using the VHS to enhance $T_{Cmax}$ and identify its location in other superconducting hydrides. Using the same theoretical tools, our analysis on the LDA level shows an enhancement of $T_{Cmax}$ in LDA calculations of $T_{Cmax, H_3Se} = 223 K}$, H$_3Se-$Pd system.

This technical report outlines a novel motion planning algorithm, addressing the limitations of existing methods in coping with large query counts when using sampling-based algorithms in dynamic environments. One major issue with these algorithms is the inability of many sampling-based algorithms to efficiently stop exploring inferior samples when the motion planning process involves large numbers of invalid samples. To mitigate this problem, our algorithm applies a 3D spatial restriction mechanism to diminish the size of the motion planning search space, thereby reducing the rate of invalid samples and minimizing the associated overhead. The evaluation involved using our algorithm on three dynamic pathfinding problems: mobile robot navigation, autonomous vehicle routing, and autonomous vehicle routing with constraints on energy efficiency, while the experimental results showed that our algorithm significantly outperformed state-of-the-art sampling-based algorithms in finding motion plans, with top-ranked results in 87% and bottom-ranked results in 13% of the cases. The reduction in the number of nodes to be processed by our algorithm was found to be directly proportional to its spatial restriction parameter. The algorithm's spatial restriction mechanism is easily exportable to other motion planning problems, with the exception of those that inherently consider spatial constraints. Furthermore, our algorithm is applicable to any motion planning problem with a well-defined search space.

This research proposes a method for visual relocalization based on 3D surface mapping, incorporating an artificially generated dataset to simulate real 3D maps and demonstrate the significance of accurate 3D mapping. Our approach starts by creating a metric 3D map in an a priori manner, then determines the point cloud's origin by matching the observed 3D features with the preconstructed map. Furthermore, this technique incorporates a neural network to simulate human object detection and improves the stability of feature matching by utilizing a weighted voting strategy over multiple orientations. The proposed method was tested on the benchmark dataset without artificial restrictions and compared with state-of-the-art monocular localization techniques that employ learned descriptors. The results indicate that our approach achieves a reasonable 3D mapping accuracy and demonstrates competitive performance compared to the existing descriptors on the benchmark dataset. When combined with a depth estimator, this method has been shown to successfully navigate an environment with our mobile robot platform.

In MIMO broadcast systems, user selection and precoding are crucial aspects. Current research typically addresses these problems separately, with user selection being modeled as an integer programming issue and precoding as an optimization problem. This paper presents a combined approach, applying a Group LASSO technique to achieve a joint user choice and precoding solution. By transforming the integer programming problem into a continuous Group LASSO problem, we can leverage the strengths of modern sparse optimization methods. The proposed method is evaluated under a specific channel model and demonstrates substantial benefits in terms of sum-rate improvement, particularly with increased numbers of users and antennas.

We demonstrate that there is a finite collection $\mathcal{S}$ of semifield arrangements such that any rational function semifield established on a tropical curve $\mathcal{C}$ can be constructed from an arrangement of $\mathcal{S}$ applied to $\mathcal{C}$.

We establish that for any fixed $x$, the difference between the quantile function $Q(\lambda,x)$ and the standard cumulative distribution function $\Phi$ becomes arbitrarily small at $x$, given that $\lambda$ approaches infinity. The rate of this convergence is uniform for all $x$ in the interval $[-\infty,+\infty]$. Building on this, we show that a compound Poisson process with payment amounts drawn from a fixed set converges in distribution to a normal process with the same mean and variance as the quantile function $Q(\lambda,x)$. The same result holds for non-standard payment distributions that tend to corresponding standard normal quantiles as the number of elements in the set approaches infinity. In addition, we derive an upper limit for the difference between the quantile function $Q(\lambda,x)$ and the standard normal quantile function $\Phi(x)$. The results have been validated through numerical examples.

We've demonstrated that manipulating a specific four-dimensional cube called a 2-2 Coxeter diagram, known as a diagram of order two, can be broken down into a series of two separate manipulations, each involving the application of a Fox-Hatcher loop. One of these operations transforms the loop in a way that's equivalent to a push-through move along a line, while the other transforms it into a push-through move along a plane. It has been discovered that a specific type of mathematical invariant, which is based on the Fox-Harten loop and operates with an order of three, exists in a particular region of the Fox-Harten loop's space. This has led to the confirmation of a hypothesis put forth by the triologist, Cook. This new invariant, which is referred to as Cook's trioid invariant, holds significant meaning in a particular type of mathematical model, which is based on a loop and referred to as a Vassiliev invariant. This model operates with an order of three. When examining the properties of the Fox-Harten loop, it was discovered that a particular type of mathematical model, which is referred to as a bivariant, plays a crucial role in understanding its behavior. This bivariant model, which is referred to as the'second Vassiliev invariant', has been completely defined and provides a critical component in the creation of Cook's trioid invariant.
